processing: Fixed, rolled, first dried, shaped into strips, worked to raise the down and finally dried, about 50 minutes in all for top grades.
harvest_season: Picking starts around Qingming in early April, one bud with one leaf about 3 cm long. Purple buds, damaged and rain-wet leaves are left out.
appearance_dry: Tight, slender, eyebrow-curved strips, glossy green with visible white down.
appearance_liquor: Clear pale green with a faint yellow tint.
appearance_wet: Even green leaves that open out flat.
taste_profile: High, long-lasting aroma with a fresh, rich cup.

brewing.notes: General green tea advice: downy leaf can cloud the first steep a little, which is normal.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest, with lots picked before Qingming the most sought after locally. Drink it within the year, as with other green teas.
description:
Huaguoshan Yunwu is a green tea from Huaguo Mountain near Lianyungang, in the far north of Jiangsu near the sea. It is also sold as Yuntaishan Yunwu after the wider range, and the mountain will be familiar to readers of Journey to the West. Yunwu means cloud and mist, a name shared with many Chinese teas.

The gardens are on slopes at around 500 metres, and the ones west of Shuilian Cave are especially well regarded. Top lots are one bud and one leaf, about 3 cm long, needing 60,000 to 70,000 shoots for a jin of finished tea.

The strips are tight and slightly curved like an eyebrow, with white down over a glossy green. The liquor is clear and pale green, and the taste is fresh and full with a lasting aroma. It takes slightly hotter water than the finest bud greens, around 85 degrees.

This is a northern tea, so its spring comes late compared with the south. Look for the harvest date, and for the geographical indication if you want the local article rather than a generic cloud and mist tea.
history:
The usual account has local growers first making the tea in the Song dynasty and sending it as tribute, which is hard to verify and rests on later retellings. The Yuntai range has long been known as a tea mountain, and the tea is cited in the local gazetteer Yuntai Xinzhi and in a Jiangsu tea assessment of 1934.

Today it is a protected name with a national geographical indication, and the local trade has extended from growing into processing and tea tourism.
